Distinguished Chairman and distinguished delegates, the Commission on Narcotic Drugs remains the most valuable global forum for advancing our shared international drug policy commitments. Australia, as a trusted world-leading producer of opiates for pharmaceutical purposes, remains committed to the integrity of the international drug control framework. The continued presence of synthetic drugs and new psychoactive substances in our local markets presents ongoing social health and security challenges. Australia is implementing a series of initiatives to address these challenges, including through the establishment of our prompt response network. For delegates wanting to know more about our prompt response network, we are hosting a hybrid side event that explores the public health applications of early warning systems 30 am. We thank Brazil, New Zealand and the Netherlands for their involvement. Chair and distinguished delegates, methamphetamine remains the drug posing the greatest challenge to Australia and our region. Australia is working closely with regional partners to detect, deter and disrupt drug trafficking by transnational serious and organised crime groups. Through programs like the Mekong Australia Partnership on Transnational Crime, the Pacific Policing Initiative, and our support for UNODC's safe handling and drug disposal work in Southeast Asia, we are building deeper and stronger cooperation across the Indo-Pacific to combat this shared challenge. Australia recently launched a new wastewater drug monitoring program in Fiji. which reflects the shared commitment of both nations to improving community safety and public health through innovative evidence-based approaches. Increases in methamphetamine availability coupled with unsafe injecting drug practices have been attributed to an alarming growth in numbers of HIV transmission in our region. Australia is supporting efforts in Southeast Asia and the Pacific to address the transmission of blood-borne viruses through contributions to the Global Fund and through the new Australian Support for Pacific HIV Action initiative. Evidence-based harm reduction interventions such as needle and syringe programs alongside sustained efforts to reduce stigma and discrimination associated with HIV and drug use remain essential to effective responses. Distinguished Chair and distinguished delegates, Australia reiterates the importance of ensuring responses to address the world drug situation are evidence informed, respect human rights and gender equality, and consider broader determinants. This requires meaningful and sustained engagement with all relevant stakeholders, including civil society organisations and affected communities. Further, Australia underscores that there is no conclusive evidence that the death penalty deters drug-related offences, and we will continue to call for its abolition in all circumstances and for all people. As we work towards our review in 2029, We must consider our international drug policy commitments, human rights obligations and commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development to be compatible, complementary and mutually reinforcing.
